title: On-Call Rotation: How to Design a Schedule for Small Teams
summary:
This guide was written by Arthur Azrieli, CTO at MeteorOps, and first published on the MeteorOps blog.

Bottom line

An on-call rotation is a schedule that names one engineer (the primary) to answer production pages for a fixed period, usually one week, with a secondary as backup and a clear escalation path above them. For a small team, the right rotation is weekly primary and secondary, paging only on customer impact, with written handoffs and runbooks.

You do not need a Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) team to run on-call well. You need named owners, a schedule people can actually sustain, alerts that only fire when a human must act, and an escalation policy that gets the right person involved without a debate at 3 a.m. This guide covers each of those for teams of 3 to 15 engineers: rotation types, team-size math, escalation rules, paging hygiene, handoffs, compensation and tooling, plus a schedule template you can copy.

On-call rotation basics: primary, secondary and escalation

Every working rotation has the same three layers, whatever tool you use:

  • Primary on-call: receives every page first, acknowledges it, and owns the first response: triage, mitigation, and calling for help.

  • Secondary on-call: is paged automatically if the primary does not acknowledge in time, and joins any incident that needs a second pair of hands.

  • Escalation contact: usually an engineering lead or CTO, who joins for customer-facing outages, security incidents, and decisions with business risk such as rolling back a migration or putting the product into read-only mode.

A shift is the period one person holds the primary pager. The rotation is the order in which people take shifts. The schedule is the rotation laid out on a calendar with overrides for holidays and sick days. When people search for "on call schedule" they usually want the last one, so there is a template further down.

Rotation types compared

Pick the rotation type from your team size and where your engineers live, not from what a large company does. These are the patterns that work in practice:

Rotation type How it works Good for Watch out for
Weekly primary only One person holds the pager for 7 days, then hands over Teams of 3 to 4 with low page volume No backup when the primary is unreachable; burnout if pages are frequent
Weekly primary and secondary This week's secondary becomes next week's primary Most teams of 4 to 10 Each person holds a pager 2 weeks out of every N
Business hours plus best effort Formal paging only during working hours; nights are best effort or limited to SEV1 Very small teams, B2B products with daytime usage Must be agreed with leadership and reflected in customer commitments
Weekday and weekend split One person covers Monday to Friday, another covers the weekend Teams where weekend load is low but non-zero Weekend shifts feel heavier; rotate them fairly
Follow the sun Two or three regions each cover their own daytime, 8 to 12 hours each Teams spread across time zones with at least 2 to 3 people per region Handoff quality between regions becomes the main failure point
Service-based rotations Each team carries its own pager for the services it owns Organizations with several product teams and clear ownership Needs a cross-team escalation path for shared infrastructure

Default recommendation for a startup: weekly primary and secondary, handover on a weekday morning (never Friday evening or Monday 9 a.m.), with paging limited to customer impact. Move to follow the sun only when you genuinely have people awake in another region.

How many engineers you need for a sustainable rotation

Rotation math is simple, and it is the most common thing teams get wrong. With a weekly rotation of N people, each person is primary one week in N. Add a secondary and each person holds a pager 2 weeks in N.

Engineers in rotation Primary weeks per year (each) Pager weeks per year with secondary (each) Verdict
2 26 52 Not sustainable for 24/7. Use business hours only.
3 about 17 about 35 Fragile. One vacation breaks it.
4 13 26 Workable if pages are rare.
6 about 9 about 17 Comfortable for most startups.
8 6.5 13 Healthy for 24/7 from one site.

Google's SRE book gives two reference points that hold up well outside Google: on-call should take no more than 25% of an engineer's time, and a 24/7 rotation from a single site needs at least eight engineers (six per site for a two-site follow-the-sun setup). It also suggests a ceiling of about two incidents per 12-hour shift, because each real incident takes hours once you include the follow-up. See Being On-Call in the Google SRE book.

If you are below those numbers, that is normal for a startup. Compensate by narrowing what pages (customer impact only), shortening the paging window, and widening the rotation: include every engineer who ships to production, not just the "infra person".

Severity levels and paging rules

Paging rules decide whether on-call is tolerable. Agree on severity before the first bad night, then map each level to a response:

Severity Example Response
SEV1 Checkout, login or the core API is down for most users; data loss risk; security incident Page primary immediately, 24/7. Escalate to secondary after 5 minutes without acknowledgement.
SEV2 Partial degradation, one region or a subset of customers affected, a critical background job stopped Page during the agreed coverage window; otherwise notify the on-call channel.
SEV3 Elevated errors below customer impact thresholds, a flaky job, a degraded internal tool Ticket for the next working day. Never pages at night.
SEV4 Noisy alert, cleanup, known bug Backlog.

The 5 minute acknowledgement for user-facing services and around 30 minutes for less time-critical systems match the response targets in the Google SRE book. Pick numbers your team can meet consistently; a promise of 5 minutes that is missed every second weekend is worse than an honest 15.

Every page should pass three tests: it reflects customer impact or imminent risk of it, the on-call engineer can take a concrete action, and the alert carries enough context to start (service, environment, severity, dashboard link, runbook link, recent deploys). "CPU above 80% for 5 minutes" usually fails all three. "Login error rate above 2% for 5 minutes in production" passes. If your team already ignores alerts, fix that before building the rotation; our guide to handling alert fatigue covers how.


An alert that fails any of the three tests belongs in a ticket or the backlog, not on someone's phone at night.

Escalation policy example

An escalation policy is the ordered list of who gets paged, and when, if nobody acknowledges. Write it down in your paging tool and in the runbook. A good default for a small team:

Escalation policy: production-critical
Level 1: current primary on-call
         page by push + SMS + phone call
         escalate if not acknowledged in 5 minutes
Level 2: current secondary on-call
         escalate if not acknowledged in 10 minutes
Level 3: engineering lead (or CTO)
Repeat:  restart at level 1 up to 2 times

Escalation policy: business-hours
Level 1: current primary on-call, push notification only
         Mon to Fri, 09:00 to 18:00 local time
Outside hours: post to #oncall, create a ticket

Also write down when the primary should escalate by choice, not just by timeout: the incident affects paying customers, the failing component is not clear after 15 minutes, a rollback risks data inconsistency, the fix needs access the primary does not have, or the same alert keeps firing after mitigation. Escalating early is a skill, not a failure.


Each level only gets paged when the one before it stays silent, so a missed page never ends with nobody responding.

On-call schedule template

Copy this for a six-person team running weekly primary and secondary, with handover on Wednesday at 10:00. Wednesday handovers keep both people at work for the handoff and avoid starting a shift on a weekend.

Week starting (Wed 10:00) Primary Secondary Notes
Week 1 Engineer A Engineer B
Week 2 Engineer B Engineer C
Week 3 Engineer C Engineer D Release freeze, extra care
Week 4 Engineer D Engineer E
Week 5 Engineer E Engineer F Public holiday Thursday: override to Engineer A
Week 6 Engineer F Engineer A

Rules that keep it fair: swaps are allowed if both people agree and the tool is updated, holidays are distributed across the year, nobody is primary two weeks in a row, and new joiners shadow one full shift as an extra secondary before taking primary.


Each engineer spends a week as backup before taking the pager, so they start their primary week already aware of what is going on.

Handoff checklist

A five-minute handoff prevents most "nobody told me" incidents. The outgoing primary posts this in the on-call channel:

  • Incidents and pages from the past shift, and anything still open.

  • Deploys, migrations or config changes that changed production behavior.

  • Known degraded dependencies, temporary alerts, or silenced monitors (with expiry).

  • Upcoming risky work: launches, load tests, database maintenance.

  • Alerts that fired but were not actionable, so they get fixed instead of ignored.

Runbooks and access for the person holding the pager

The on-call engineer should never need to ask "am I allowed to roll this back?" Write runbooks for the incidents you can predict, starting with the top five by frequency: roll back a bad deploy, restart or scale a stuck worker, handle database connection exhaustion, investigate a spike in API errors, rotate a leaked secret. Each runbook needs symptoms, first checks, safe mitigations, risky actions to avoid, and who to call.

Access is the part teams forget. The primary needs enough access to diagnose and mitigate, but standing admin access for everyone is how incidents get worse. The pattern that works: read access to logs, metrics and cluster state for everyone in the rotation, plus time-limited elevated access (just-in-time roles, or an audited break-glass role) that the on-call engineer can grant themselves during an incident. This also answers a common question: you can remove standing production access from the team without breaking on-call, as long as the elevation path is tested before you need it.


Read access lets anyone diagnose, and elevation is granted only for the incident that needs it.

On-call compensation and burnout

On-call is work outside normal hours, and teams that treat it as free eventually lose their most reliable engineers. The common compensation models are:

  • Flat stipend per shift: a fixed amount for each week on primary, regardless of pages. Simple and predictable.

  • Per-incident or hourly pay: paid for time actually spent responding outside hours. Fairer when load is uneven, more admin.

  • Time off in lieu: a late-morning start or a day off after a rough night. Cheap and often the most appreciated.

  • Combination: a small stipend plus time off after any night page.

Labor rules on standby time vary by country, so check local requirements before you set a policy. Beyond money, the strongest burnout controls are operational: track pages per shift, review every night page in a weekly on-call review, and give the on-call engineer explicit permission to spend quiet shift time fixing the alerts that woke them up.

On-call tools: what each is good at

The tool matters less than the policy, but the tool should make schedules, overrides and escalations easy to see and change.

Tool Strength Note
PagerDuty Mature scheduling, escalation policies and integrations The reference product; cost grows with team size
incident.io On-call plus incident workflow inside Slack Strong if incidents already run in Slack
Grafana Cloud IRM On-call and incident response next to Grafana dashboards and alerts Natural fit if you already use Grafana
Rootly, FireHydrant Incident management with on-call scheduling Compare their paging reliability and pricing for your size
Opsgenie Long-time PagerDuty alternative Atlassian ended new sales on June 4, 2025 and shuts it down on April 5, 2027; plan a migration (Atlassian notice)

Whatever you choose, test it: trigger a test page to each person's phone during onboarding, confirm phone-call escalation works with Do Not Disturb on, and review the schedule for gaps every month.

Common on-call mistakes in small teams

  • One hero on permanent call. The person who built the infrastructure answers every page. It feels efficient until they leave or burn out.

  • Paging on symptoms nobody can act on. Resource alerts without user impact train people to ignore the pager.

  • No secondary. A dead phone battery becomes a full outage.

  • Handover on Monday morning. The outgoing person is already in planning meetings and the handoff gets skipped.

  • Runbooks that live in someone's head. The first incident handled by a new engineer becomes a guessing game.

  • No review of pages. The same noisy alert wakes someone every week and nothing changes.

A 30-day plan to launch on-call before you hire SRE

  1. Week 1: list your production services and name an owner for each. Agree severity levels and the paging window with leadership.

  2. Week 2: audit alerts. Delete or downgrade anything that does not pass the three tests. Add the missing customer-impact alerts (error rate, latency, failed critical jobs).

  3. Week 3: set up the schedule and escalation policy in your tool, write the top five runbooks, and set up just-in-time elevated access.

  4. Week 4: run a game day: trigger a realistic failure in staging and have the primary handle it end to end. Fix what was confusing, then go live.


Alerts get fixed before the schedule goes live, so the first real shift starts with pages worth answering.

Plan to revisit after the first month: pages per shift, time to acknowledge, and which alerts woke people for nothing. When the rotation itself becomes the bottleneck, that is the signal to formalize the role; our guide on how to build a DevOps team covers that decision.

On-call rotation FAQ

Start with a weekly primary and secondary rotation that includes every engineer who ships to production, page only on customer impact, and hand over midweek with a short written checklist. With fewer than four people, limit formal paging to business hours plus SEV1 at night.

How does an on-call schedule work?

The schedule assigns shifts on a calendar, the paging tool routes alerts to whoever is on shift, and overrides cover holidays and swaps. If the primary does not acknowledge within the agreed time, the escalation policy pages the secondary, then a lead.

How long should an on-call shift be?

One week is the most common and works well for small teams because it limits handovers. Follow-the-sun teams use 8 to 12 hour shifts per region. Avoid shifts longer than a week unless pages are very rare.

Should engineers be paid for on-call?

Most companies compensate on-call through a stipend per shift, pay for time spent on incidents, time off in lieu, or a mix. Unpaid on-call with frequent night pages is one of the fastest ways to lose senior engineers, and local labor rules may require compensation.

No. Product engineers can run a healthy rotation if ownership, alerting, runbooks and escalation are in place. An SRE function becomes worth it when reliability work consistently competes with product work and the rotation is large enough to need dedicated ownership.

Google's SRE guidance puts the minimum at eight engineers for a single-site 24/7 rotation, or six per site for two sites. Smaller teams can still cover 24/7 by keeping night paging to true emergencies and keeping page volume low.

If you need production covered before your team is big enough to carry a pager sustainably, MeteorOps provides SRE on-call support that plugs into your existing rotation and tooling.

title: Your Build Scripts Still Run VBScript and Windows Is Switching It Off
summary:
Somewhere in your company
there is a file
ending in dot vbs.

Probably more than one.

A logon script
that maps the shared drives.

A scheduled task
that zips last night's exports.

A build step
nobody has opened since
the person who wrote it left.

An Excel macro
that borrows VBScript's
regular expressions
to clean up a column.

They all run today,
through cscript or wscript,
the way they have
for twenty years.

That is ending,
on a published schedule.

In 2023
Microsoft announced
that VBScript is deprecated.

In 2024
it laid out three phases.

First,
from Windows 11 version 24H2,
VBScript becomes an optional feature,
installed and on by default.

Nothing breaks.

That is the phase
you are in now.

Second,
around 2027,
it stays available
but is no longer on by default.

New machines,
fresh images,
rebuilt servers
arrive without it.

Third,
at a date not yet given,
it is removed,
DLLs and all.

The danger is phase two.

It will show up first
where machines are new.

On the laptop
for the next starter,
whose drives do not map
on the first morning.

On the rebuilt build agent
where a step that has always passed
fails,
with an error
that names a file
nobody remembers.

On the finance PC
where the macro stops
at the first line
that touches the regex object.

Nothing will warn you
the day before.

So go looking now,
while it still works,
because working code
is easy to read.

Search shares,
group policy,
scheduled tasks,
repositories
and build definitions
for dot vbs,
cscript
and wscript.

Search your Office files
for the VBScript
regular expressions reference.

Then build one test machine
with the optional feature
turned off,
and run your real start of day
on it.

title: How to use your root domain (example.com) as a custom domain
summary:
By Octave · drafted with AI, tested on Hubfly space. Originally published on the Hubfly space blog.

TL;DR

  • What you get: your app answering on your-domain.com and www.your-domain.com, with HTTPS that renews itself.
  • Who it's for: anyone launching a product site, shop or SaaS on its own name.
  • Time: about 10 minutes of clicking, plus however long your DNS provider takes to publish records (minutes to a few hours).
  • Cost: the domain connection and certificate are free on Hubfly space. You only pay for the app itself, and small apps fit in the free tier.

Your app works on a long platform address, and you've bought your-domain.com. Then you hit the wall every launch hits: the subdomain (www) connects in two minutes, but the bare domain won't take a CNAME record. Visitors who type your name without www get an error page, and that's the version people put on business cards.

In this guide you'll connect both, prove you own the domain, and get HTTPS on both names without touching a certificate. It takes one TXT record, one or two routing records, and a click. Try it on Hubfly space while you read; the free tier includes 360 runtime hours a month.

Why the root domain is the hard part

DNS has a rule: a name that has a CNAME record can't have any other record. Your root domain (written @ in most DNS panels) always has other records, like the SOA and NS records that make the domain work, and usually MX records for email. So most providers refuse a CNAME at @. Even where they let you type one, it can break your email.

Providers work around this in two ways:

  • ALIAS or ANAME records (offered by Namecheap, DNSimple and others): they behave like a CNAME but are answered as normal address records.
  • A records: a fixed IP address. Every DNS provider supports them.

Hubfly space accepts an ALIAS, ANAME or A record at @. The value to use is shown in your domain's setup modal in the dashboard, so always copy it from there rather than from a blog post (including this one).

Step 1: Add your domain and prove you own it

Before Hubfly space routes any traffic for a name, it checks that the name is yours. This stops someone else from claiming your domain on the platform.

  1. Open dashboard.hubfly.space and click Domains in the bottom navigation bar.
  2. Under Add domain, type your bare domain, for example your-domain.com, and click Add.
  3. The domain appears under Your domains with the status Pending, and the Configuration panel shows one TXT record to create.

The Domains page after adding a domain: a Pending status and the TXT record that proves ownership.

The record looks like this. Copy both values with the copy buttons rather than retyping them:

Type Host / Name Value
TXT _hubfly-verification (full name _hubfly-verification.your-domain.com) hubfly-verify=
  1. In your DNS provider, add that TXT record. Many panels add your domain automatically, so type only _hubfly-verification in the Host field. If you paste the full name, some providers save _hubfly-verification.your-domain.com.your-domain.com, and verification never passes.
  2. Back in Hubfly space, click Verify Connection.

If the record isn't visible yet, the panel says exactly what it looked for:

The message you see when the TXT record isn't published yet.

"Could not find TXT record matching …" means the record isn't public yet or the host is wrong. Wait a few minutes and click Verify Connection again. You can check it yourself from a terminal:

dig +short TXT _hubfly-verification.your-domain.com

When the command prints your hubfly-verify=… value, verification will pass.

Step 2: Attach the domain to your app or load balancer

A verified domain still needs a destination. Hubfly space can send it to a single container or to a load balancer.

  • Single container: open your project, select the container and open its Networking tab, where you expose your app's port over HTTP and attach your domain.
  • Load balancer: if you run several copies of your app, put the domain on the load balancer instead. In the load balancer editor (Topology Studio), ingress domains are wired on the left and your backend containers on the right, so one domain spreads traffic across all of them.

Add www.your-domain.com on the Domains page the same way and attach it too, so both names reach your app.

Step 3: Point DNS at Hubfly space

Now tell the internet where to send visitors. Use the exact values from your domain's setup modal in the dashboard:

Name Record type Value
@ (root) ALIAS, ANAME or A the value in your domain's setup modal
www CNAME the target in your domain's setup modal

If your provider has no ALIAS or ANAME record type, use the A record option. Some providers (Cloudflare, for example) also offer "CNAME flattening" at the root; check that your provider can flatten to the value the dashboard gives you before relying on it.

Keep your existing MX and email TXT records. You're adding records, not replacing the zone.

Step 4: Let HTTPS set itself up

Once DNS points at Hubfly space, the TLS certificate is provisioned automatically and renewed 30 days before it expires. There's no cron job and nothing to upload. When DNS has propagated, open https://your-domain.com and https://www.your-domain.com to check both names.

Pick one name as the main one for search engines and redirect the other to it, so Google doesn't index two copies of your site. Most frameworks do this in a few lines of middleware.

FAQ: can I just use a CNAME at the root?

Usually not. A CNAME can't share a name with other records, and your root always has some. Use ALIAS, ANAME or an A record at @, and keep the CNAME for www.

What can go wrong

  1. "Could not find TXT record matching …". The record isn't published yet, or the host was saved with your domain twice. Check with dig (above), fix the host, wait, and verify again.
  2. The site still shows your old host after the switch. Your old A or CNAME record is still in place, or resolvers have cached it. Delete the old record for that name, keep only the one from Step 3, and give caches time to expire.
  3. Your email stops working after the change. You replaced the root records instead of adding to them, or forced a plain CNAME at @. Restore your MX and SPF records and use an ALIAS, ANAME or A record for the root.

Limits and pricing, honestly

  • Custom domains and certificates are free. Hubfly space charges no domain or certificate fee.
  • The app is what you pay for. On the free tier you get 360 runtime hours a month, and a shared container sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic, so the first visit after a quiet spell is slower. An always-on Dedicated container with 0.5 vCPU, 512 MB RAM and 4 GB disk costs:
    • CPU: 0.5 × $0.004 × 730 h = $1.46
    • RAM: 0.5 GB × $0.002 × 730 h = $0.73
    • Disk: 4 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 h = $0.04
    • Total: about $2.23 a month.
  • Load balancers have no listed fee (free); each target container is billed as above.
  • DNS timing isn't in anyone's control. Most records show up in minutes, but providers can take hours.

Who this is not for

  • If your site must stay on servers in another cloud, keep your DNS pointed there.
  • If you need a wildcard domain (*.your-domain.com) for customer subdomains, this guide doesn't cover it.

Takeaway

The root domain only feels hard because of one DNS rule. Prove ownership with one TXT record, attach the name to your app or load balancer, use an ALIAS, ANAME or A record at @, and HTTPS takes care of itself.

  • Run several copies of your app behind one domain with weighted targets: Load balancers.
  • Give the app a database it can reach over TLS: Managed Databases.

title: Four Failure Domains
summary:
Four Failure Domains

Zone, datacenter, provider, continent: what a system feels at each level - latency, loss, a split, the whole level gone - and what the clouds themselves say about it.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

This part is conceptual. The ordering of link kinds at the end is built; the failure-scenario runs across these levels are planned, not run.

This is part 2 of the series on testing cross-zone, cross-datacenter and cross-provider behaviour on a laptop. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

One ladder

An availability zone, a datacenter, a provider and a continent sound like four separate topics. They are one ladder. Each step is a failure domain one size larger than the last, and each step up changes two things at once: how far apart the pieces are, and what can go wrong between them.

The value of seeing it as a ladder is that one design can cover all four. Copies of a service are placed on the ladder; the network between them is described by the ladder; failures are cut at a step of the ladder. Part 1, One Login For Every Stand, gave every local environment one way in. This part is the map of where the copies behind that door can live, and what each place costs.

Zone

A zone is the smallest domain that a cloud promises to keep independent. AWS describes an Availability Zone as one or more discrete data centers with separate and redundant power, networking and connectivity, far enough apart to avoid correlated failures and close enough for synchronous replication with single-digit millisecond latency (AWS).

For a system, a zone means:

  • latency - near zero; nobody designs around it;
  • loss of a zone - the copies in it are gone; a quorum spread over three zones survives one.

The second line is the whole reason for three. Two copies of three is a majority; one of two is not.

Datacenter and metro

The next step is a whole site, or a metro of sites. Latency is small but no longer zero, and it is the first step where a timeout chosen on a laptop can be wrong in production. Synchronous replication is still possible inside a metro; it is simply slower.

A datacenter lost is a zone lost, only bigger: everything in it at once, including the things that were assumed to be "elsewhere" because they were in another zone of the same site.

Provider

A provider is a different kind of step. It is not further away so much as differently owned. Everything a provider runs - its API, its DNS, its network, its control plane - can fail together, and when it does, every site of that provider goes with it.

For a link between two places, the provider question has only two answers: the same provider or a different one. That is the whole axis.

Continent

The top step is the one physics decides. Between continents the round trip is many times larger than inside a region, and no configuration makes it smaller. Google's guidance says it plainly: communication within regions will always be cheaper and faster than communication across regions (Google Cloud).

At this step synchronous replication stops being a design choice. The main risk becomes the split: a cut between two continents leaves two halves that both believe they are the system.

What a system feels

Put the four steps side by side and the effects line up:

Level Latency Loss on the link A split The whole level gone
zone near zero rare unlikely copies in it lost; a quorum of three zones holds
datacenter / metro small rare possible everything in the site at once
provider depends on placement depends on placement possible every site of that provider, its API and DNS
continent many times larger more likely the main risk half the system on the far side

The latency column reads as words, not numbers, on purpose. The order matters more than any single figure, and the order is the same in every cloud.

What the clouds say

Three providers, one picture:

  • AWS - Regions are isolated and independent from other Regions; this separation limits service failures to a single Region, and resources do not exist in another Region unless replicated (AWS).
  • Google - zones are designed to minimize correlated failures of power, cooling and networking; the recommendation is to deploy across multiple zones and multiple regions (Google Cloud).
  • Azure - a zone is a logical group of physically separate datacenters, the target round trip between zones is under about two milliseconds, and zones do not protect against the loss of a whole region (Azure).

None of them says "zones are enough". All three say: know which step of the ladder each copy is on.

A ladder a tool can read

For a test, the ladder has to become data. In our topology emulation, the kind of every link is derived from where its two ends are, in a fixed order:

intra-dc  <  intra-metro  <  intra-continent  <  inter-continent
provider:  same | cross            (continent ranks above provider)

Continent ranks above provider: two sites of different providers on one continent are closer than two sites of one provider on different continents. The provider is only ever "same" or "cross". That ordering is built; how it is used is part 3.

On a laptop

On a laptop each step of the ladder is a network: a subnet for a zone, a larger one for a site, a rule for every link between them. The failures become commands: take a zone down, isolate a site, cut a continent off. The runs of those scenarios are planned - the owner postponed them - so this part stops at the map.

What I do not claim

  • Not that any of these failures has been run across the levels. They are planned.
  • Not exact latencies for any level. The order is the point; the numbers belong to each cloud's documentation.
  • Not that a laptop network behaves like a cloud network. It is an emulation, and part 3 says how close it got.

What of this is method

  • One ladder, four steps. Zone, site, provider and continent are one design, not four.
  • Know the step of every copy. A quorum is only as good as where its members are.
  • Make the ladder data. A test tool can only break what it can read.

Cross-anything on a laptop - Part 2. Next: A Planet On A Laptop.

If you spread copies across zones, do you know which site each zone is in? If you run on two providers, what fails together that you thought would not? If you have lived through a continent split, which side kept writing? Which step of the ladder does your system assume will never fail?

import sys
import urllib.request
from collections import defaultdict, deque
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.parse import urljoin, urldefrag, urlparse

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (link-check script)"}

class Links(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.links = []
    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag == "a":
            href = dict(attrs).get("href")
            if href:
                self.links.append(href)

def get(url, method="GET"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA, method=method)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
            ctype = r.headers.get("Content-Type", "")
            body = r.read() if method == "GET" and "html" in ctype else b""
            return r.status, body
    except HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, b""
    except (URLError, TimeoutError) as e:
        return f"error: {getattr(e, 'reason', e)}", b""

    host = urlparse(start).netloc
    found_on = defaultdict(set)          # link -> pages that contain it
    queue, seen, pages = deque([start]), {start}, 0
    while queue and pages < max_pages:
        page = queue.popleft()
        code, body = get(page)
        pages += 1
        p = Links()
        p.feed(body.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
        for href in p.links:
            link = urldefrag(urljoin(page, href))[0]
            if not link.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
                continue                 # mailto:, tel:, javascript:
            found_on[link].add(page)
            if urlparse(link).netloc == host and link not in seen:
                seen.add(link)
                queue.append(link)
    return found_on

    code, _ = get(link, "HEAD")
    if isinstance(code, str) or code >= 400:   # many servers mishandle HEAD: confirm with GET
        code, _ = get(link)
    return link, code

        results = list(pool.map(check, found_on))
    broken = [(l, c) for l, c in results if isinstance(c, str) or c >= 400]
    print(f"checked {len(results)} links, {len(broken)} broken")
    for link, code in broken:

The first version of my script sent only HEAD requests and flagged links that load fine in a browser. These are the usual causes:

title: NDIS Funding Changes 2026: What Participants Need to Know
summary:
The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is undergoing significant changes in 2026. These reforms are intended to improve the long-term sustainability of the scheme while changing how certain support budgets are calculated and managed.

For participants, families and carers, understanding these updates is important when preparing for a plan reassessment, reviewing support arrangements or choosing a disability support provider.

One of the most important developments is the funding reset that began on 1 October 2026. However, the changes do not affect every NDIS support category. Essential day-to-day assistance remains protected under the announced funding adjustments.

This guide explains the key NDIS funding changes in 2026, what participants should review and how to maintain continuity of everyday support.

What Are the Major NDIS Changes in 2026?

The Australian Government passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Act 2026 in August 2026.

The reforms introduce changes to funding, plan reassessments, provider compliance and the way the scheme operates.

One of the most significant changes is the reset of funding allocations for two support categories:

  • Social, Economic and Community Participation.
  • Improved Daily Living Skills.

The announced budget reset includes a 50% reduction in allocations for Social, Economic and Community Participation and a 10% reduction for Improved Daily Living Skills.

These are changes to budget allocations, not an automatic reduction in every participant's actual spending or all their NDIS funding. The impact will depend on individual circumstances and the supports included in a plan.

When Will the NDIS Funding Changes Apply?

The funding changes are being introduced progressively over 12 months.

The new allocations apply:

  • From 1 October 2026 when a new plan is approved or an existing plan is reassessed.
  • From 1 February 2027 when plans are renewed.

Participants do not all experience the changes on the same date. Existing participants can continue using their current plans and supports until their plans are reassessed or renewed.

This makes it important to understand your plan's dates rather than assume that every funding change applies immediately.

Which NDIS Supports May Be Affected?

The funding reset applies to the two identified budget categories.

1. Social, Economic and Community Participation

This category can include eligible supports that help participants access community activities, develop social connections and participate in everyday community life.

Participants who rely on these supports should review their current arrangements and consider how their goals can be achieved within the revised budget.

2. Improved Daily Living Skills

This category can include eligible capacity-building supports that help participants develop skills and greater independence.

Examples may involve therapy and assessment services, depending on the participant's plan and the applicable support rules.

Participants should check how their funded services are classified rather than assuming that every daily living service is affected.

Are Essential Daily Living Supports Still Funded?

Yes. The October 2026 budget reset does not automatically reduce all essential daily living supports.

The Government has identified several day-to-day supports that are not affected by these particular budget reductions, including assistance with:

  • Eating and drinking.
  • Dressing and toileting.
  • Laundry and cleaning.
  • Medication assistance and nursing care.
  • Home and vehicle modifications.
  • Personal mobility equipment.

This distinction is particularly important for participants who depend on regular support to manage everyday activities at home.

Eligible personal care services Melbourne participants use and assistance with daily living NDIS Melbourne services should be considered according to the participant's plan, support needs and applicable funding rules.

What Should NDIS Participants Do Now?

Understanding your funding is the first step. Participants can take practical steps to prepare for changes.

Review Your Current NDIS Plan

Check the funding categories, allocated budgets, plan dates and supports you currently use.

Identify which services fall under Social, Economic and Community Participation or Improved Daily Living Skills.

Discuss Your Support Requirements

Speak with your support coordinator, plan manager or my NDIS contact about any concerns.

If you expect your plan to be reassessed or renewed, discuss how the revised budget allocations may affect your arrangements.

Keep Relevant Documentation

Maintain reports, assessments and records that explain your disability-related support needs.

Documenting how assistance contributes to daily routines, safety and independence can help when discussing your support requirements.

Review Your Service Provider

title: Fleet Maintenance Alerts Fire Twice: Deduplicating OBD-II Fault Codes in a Telematics Backend
summary:
A fleet maintenance alert should help a technician decide what needs attention. It should not force the maintenance team to investigate the same engine fault three times because a telematics device retransmitted a message, a vehicle reported the same diagnostic code through two channels, or a backend retry created a duplicate notification.

This problem often appears when a fleet management platform begins connecting vehicles from different manufacturers, aftermarket OBD-II devices, and telematics providers. The initial implementation may work well with a small number of vehicles. As the number of connected assets grows, duplicate fault events can overwhelm dashboards, inflate notification counts, and weaken trust in automated maintenance workflows.

The solution is not simply to ignore repeated diagnostic trouble codes. A reliable backend needs to distinguish duplicate messages from recurring faults, continuing faults, and truly new incidents.

Why OBD-II Fault Codes Generate Duplicate Alerts

OBD-II systems expose diagnostic information that can help fleet operators identify engine and emissions-related problems. Depending on the vehicle, diagnostic interface, and telematics provider, the backend may receive fault information at different intervals or through different event formats.

Several conditions can produce repeated messages.

Device retransmission: A tracker temporarily loses network connectivity and sends buffered messages after reconnecting.

Webhook retries: A telematics provider retries a delivery because the receiving API did not acknowledge the original request within the expected time.

Polling overlap: A backend polls the same vehicle repeatedly and receives an unchanged diagnostic code.

Multiple data sources: A vehicle's OEM telematics feed and an aftermarket device report the same underlying fault.

Repeated fault observations: The vehicle continues reporting an active code over multiple trips. These observations may represent one ongoing incident rather than multiple new maintenance cases.

The challenge is that these situations can look similar at the message level while requiring different treatment in the maintenance system.

Start With Event Identity, Not Notification Logic

A common implementation checks whether a diagnostic code already exists for a vehicle. If it does, the backend discards the incoming event.

That approach can suppress useful information.

Consider a vehicle that reports a diagnostic code on Monday. The technician investigates and closes the maintenance case on Tuesday. The same code appears again on Friday.

If the system permanently deduplicates that vehicle-code combination, it may suppress the Friday incident even though the fault has returned.

A better design separates the raw event, the fault state, the maintenance incident, and the notification.

  • Raw event: The original diagnostic observation received from a device or provider.
  • Fault state: The backend's current understanding of the code for a specific vehicle.
  • Maintenance incident: The actionable case assigned to a technician or maintenance team.
  • Notification: The message delivered to the people responsible for responding.

This separation allows the system to retain every useful observation without creating a new maintenance case or sending another notification for every repeated message.

Build a Layered Deduplication Strategy

1. Normalize incoming diagnostic events

Before deduplication, convert incoming messages into a consistent internal structure.

A normalized event may include:

  • Fleet and vehicle identifiers
  • VIN, when available and verified
  • Telematics device identifier
  • Source provider and reporting module
  • Diagnostic trouble code
  • Code status, where supported
  • Source event timestamp
  • Backend receipt timestamp
  • Device sequence number, when available
  • Relevant diagnostic data and source payload

Normalization matters because different providers may represent the same diagnostic code differently. The backend should preserve the original payload while mapping the event into a common format.

Do not assume the device identifier, vehicle identifier, and VIN are interchangeable. Devices can be replaced, vehicles can change ownership, and hardware can be reassigned.

2. Use idempotency keys for message retries

When a provider supplies a stable event ID or sequence number, use it to identify repeat deliveries of the same message.

An idempotency key can be constructed from trusted source fields, such as the provider event ID and source account. If the provider does not supply a stable ID, a carefully designed fingerprint may combine the vehicle, source, diagnostic code, event time, and relevant status fields.

The fingerprint must reflect the source's actual behavior. A timestamp alone is rarely sufficient because devices may have clock drift, and several distinct events can occur close together.

Store processed event identifiers with a uniqueness constraint. When the same event arrives again, the backend should acknowledge it without repeating the business operation.

3. Track active fault episodes

Message deduplication cannot determine whether a fault is still active or has returned after resolution. That requires a state model.

For each vehicle and normalized fault identity, maintain a record containing fields such as:

  • Current status
  • First observed time
  • Last observed time
  • Last notification time
  • Associated maintenance case
  • Resolution or clear time, where known
  • Source observations and event history

Repeated observations can update the last-seen timestamp and diagnostic history. They do not automatically need to create a new incident.

When a fault is confirmed as cleared and later reappears, the system can open a new episode according to the relevant code's rules.

A missing observation should not automatically mean a fault has cleared. A disconnected device may simply have stopped sending data.

4. Separate fault severity from duplicate suppression

Not all diagnostic codes deserve the same notification policy. A recurring, low-priority warning and a potentially safety-critical fault should not be handled identically.

Use code-specific rules to determine whether the system should:

  • Update an existing incident silently
  • Notify the assigned technician
  • Escalate an unresolved incident
  • Reopen a resolved case
  • Create a new maintenance incident

Deduplication should reduce repetitive noise, not hide important changes in severity or status.

Make Event Processing Safe Under Retries

A telematics backend often has several asynchronous stages: event ingestion, normalization, persistence, rule evaluation, notification dispatch, and maintenance-system integration.

If the same message is processed by two workers simultaneously, both may decide that no incident exists and create one.

Use database transactions, unique constraints, or another concurrency-safe mechanism to enforce the incident-creation rule. A distributed lock can be useful in specific architectures, but it should not replace durable data-level safeguards.

Notification delivery needs its own idempotency mechanism. Creating one maintenance incident does not guarantee that an email, push notification, or webhook will be delivered only once.

For reliable processing, store notification intent in a transactional outbox or equivalent durable queue. A worker can dispatch the notification and record its delivery state. Since external delivery systems may still retry, use a stable notification key wherever the destination supports it.

Example: One Fault, Multiple Messages

Suppose a delivery truck reports diagnostic code P0420 through an aftermarket telematics device. The device sends the same buffered message twice, and the provider retries the webhook once.

The backend receives three messages.

A robust implementation would:

  1. Persist or identify the original event.
  2. Recognize repeated deliveries using the event ID or fingerprint.
  3. Maintain one active fault episode.
  4. Create one maintenance incident if the configured rules require it.
  5. Dispatch the initial notification once.
  6. Preserve later observations and retry details for audit purposes.

If the fault is cleared and subsequently returns, the backend evaluates the new evidence and may create another incident.

The important distinction is that three deliveries do not necessarily mean three faults, while three observations do not always mean one fault forever.

Test the Cases That Break Naive Deduplication

Before deploying the logic across a fleet, test more than a simple repeated-message scenario.

Include:

  • The same event delivered several times
  • The same code reported with different timestamps
  • Two providers reporting the same fault
  • Two distinct faults arriving almost simultaneously
  • A delayed message arriving after a newer event
  • A fault disappearing from the feed without an explicit clear event
  • A cleared fault returning days later
  • Concurrent workers processing the same vehicle
  • A notification provider timing out after accepting a message
  • A vehicle being reassigned to a different telematics device

Track duplicate-event rates, incidents created per fault episode, notification retries, processing delays, and faults reopened after resolution. These metrics help determine whether deduplication is reducing noise without hiding real maintenance needs.

What Fleet Management App Development Should Include

Fleet management app development is not limited to a map, a vehicle list, and a maintenance reminder screen. When the product consumes telematics data, its backend needs reliable event processing, fault history, configurable escalation rules, and connections to work orders and technician assignments.

A development team should understand the difference between raw telemetry and actionable operational events. It should also plan for mixed hardware, inconsistent provider payloads, intermittent connectivity, and data ownership across fleet accounts.

Recommended Fleet Software Development Companies

Dev Technosys is a fleet management software development company that builds custom fleet and logistics software, including applications that can connect operational workflows with telematics integrations, vehicle maintenance records, and management dashboards. Its 250+ professionals support software delivery across different business requirements. The project scope should explicitly define diagnostic event handling, integration responsibilities, and fault lifecycle rules.

IBM provides enterprise technology and integration capabilities that can support complex data and operational systems. Its enterprise engineering ecosystem can be relevant when telematics needs to connect with existing business platforms and analytics infrastructure.

Accenture works across enterprise software, cloud, data, and systems integration. Its delivery capabilities can be relevant to organizations modernizing fleet operations across several departments or existing technology platforms.

Final Thoughts

Duplicate OBD-II alerts are not merely a notification problem. They expose how a telematics backend identifies events, maintains fault state, and coordinates work across distributed systems.

The most reliable approach combines source-level idempotency, normalized diagnostic data, fault episode tracking, concurrency-safe incident creation, and independently controlled notification delivery.

The goal is not to suppress every repeated code. It is to make sure every message contributes to a trustworthy maintenance record while each actionable incident receives the appropriate response.

title: SCP Commands That Still Matter, and When rsync Beats Them
summary:
scp is the command everyone learns first and then quietly stops using, usually after the first time a transfer dies at 90% and has to start over. But it is still the lowest-friction way to move a file between two machines, because it needs nothing on the remote side except sshd. rsync needs rsync installed at both ends. sftp needs an interactive session or a batch file.

This is a reference for the cases where scp is genuinely the right tool, plus the exact points where it stops being one.

The two protocols hiding behind one command

Since OpenSSH 9.0 (April 2022), scp transfers files over the SFTP protocol by default. Before that, it used the old RCP-derived protocol, which had a nasty class of path-traversal bugs (CVE-2019-6110, CVE-2019-6111, CVE-2019-6109).

You can check what you are running:

ssh -V

If the result is older than 9.0, scp still uses the legacy protocol unless you force the new one:

scp -s sftp file.txt user@host:/tmp/

This matters in two practical ways. First, the legacy protocol can silently overwrite files outside the target directory when the server is malicious — not your usual threat model, but relevant if you pull from untrusted hosts. Second, the protocol change altered how some wildcard and quoting edge cases behave.

The flags you will actually type 

scp source user@host:/path/

Copy the other way:

scp user@host:/path/file.txt ./local-dir/
Flag Meaning
-P 2222 Remote port (capital P — ssh uses lowercase -p)
-r Recurse into directories
-p Preserve modification times and permissions (lowercase)
-C Compress in transit
-l 8000 Bandwidth limit in Kbit/s
-q Quiet
-i key.pem Identity file
-J bastion Jump through a bastion host (OpenSSH 7.3+)
-3 Route traffic between two remote hosts through your machine

The -p / -P collision is the single most common source of confusion. -P is the port, -p preserves attributes. Get it backwards and you will either connect to port 22 or lose your timestamps.

Copying between two remote hosts

The naive version routes the data through your laptop:

scp user1@hostA:/data/dump.sql user2@hostB:/backup/

That is -3 behaviour by default (in older OpenSSH it was the only behaviour). If both hosts can reach each other, tell scp to connect them directly:

scp -R user1@hostA:/data/dump.sql user2@hostB:/backup/

-R requires that hostA can resolve and authenticate to hostB. In a datacenter that is usually true and it is dramatically faster. Across the public internet it usually is not, and you want the -3 route instead.

Quoting is where scp hurts

scp passes the remote path to a remote shell, so the string goes through two rounds of expansion — your local shell, then the remote one. Spaces and globs need double escaping:

scp "user@host:/path/with\ spaces/file.txt" .

Then the remote glob is expanded remotely, which is what you want:

scp "user@host:/var/log/*.gz" ./logs/

But a local glob in the destination position is a common mistake:

# wrong: the star is sent to the remote shell verbatim in some versions
scp file1 file2 user@host:/backup/*

Use scp file1 file2 user@host:/backup/ and let the directory name be the target.

What scp cannot do

This is the part that pushes people to rsync, and it is worth being blunt about the limits:

  • No resume. A dropped connection means starting the file over.
  • No exclusion patterns. There is no --exclude.
  • No delta transfer. Every byte is sent, every time.
  • No dry run. You cannot preview what would change.
  • Poor feedback. One progress line per file, no aggregate ETA.

For a 400 MB log file over a flaky connection, scp is the wrong tool. For a 12 KB config file, it is the right one and rsync is overkill.

rsync as the upgrade path

The minimum useful invocation:

rsync -avz --partial --progress ./build/ user@host:/var/www/app/
  • -a = archive: recurse, preserve symlinks, permissions, times, owner/group. It implies -r -l -p -t -g -o -D.
  • -v verbose, -z compress.
  • --partial keeps a partially transferred file so a retry resumes instead of restarting. This is the flag that solves the actual scp pain point.

Exclusions, which scp has no answer for:

rsync -avz --exclude 'node_modules' --exclude '.git' --exclude '*.log' ./ user@host:/srv/app/

Dry run before a destructive sync:

rsync -avzn --delete ./ user@host:/srv/app/

-n (or --dry-run) prints what would happen. Never run --delete without -n first. A trailing-slash mistake turns rsync -a ./src host:/dst into "create /dst/src" instead of "sync the contents of src into /dst", and combined with --delete that is how people erase directories.

When the remote has no rsync

Common on appliances, minimal containers, and older NAS firmware. Two workarounds that need nothing but ssh:

Stream a tar:

tar czf - ./project | ssh user@host 'tar xzf - -C /srv/'

Resume a large file with dd:

ssh user@host 'tail -c +$(( $(stat -c%s /srv/big.iso 2>/dev/null || echo 0) + 1 ))' >> big.iso

The dd trick is fragile and easy to get wrong by one byte. If resumption matters, install rsync on the remote; it is a package in every distribution and a brew install on macOS.

SFTP when you want to look around

scp is one-shot. If you need to list, cd, and fetch several files, the interactive client is faster than chaining six scp commands:

sftp user@host

Then ls, cd, get, put, lcd, lls. Batch mode skips the prompt:

The two protocols hiding behind one command

Since OpenSSH 9.0 (April 2022), scp transfers files over the SFTP protocol by default. Before that, it used the old RCP-derived protocol, which had a nasty class of path-traversal bugs (CVE-2019-6110, CVE-2019-6111, CVE-2019-6109).

title: Idempotent Jobs & Exactly-Once Effects: Designing Safe Retries
summary:
Durable execution, async LLM workflows and message-delivery debates keep showing up on DEV: MQTT QoS posts, local agent pipelines, tool-call cost control. The fancy orchestration only works if the boring layer underneath is honest about failure. Most SaaS queues deliver at least once. Your job will run again after a worker crash, a deploy, a lock timeout or a broker redelivery. If that job charges a card, sends a welcome email or decrements inventory, "just retry" becomes double billing. Part 1 of this series is the foundation every queue needs before you chase orchestration frameworks: idempotent jobs and exactly-once effects.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every example and claim myself against Laravel queue behaviour and common BullMQ patterns. I build Loop Origin, where we design and ship Laravel and Node SaaS systems for clients, and this post opens a new series on reliable queues and async work.

📚 Series Roadmap — Reliable Queues & Async Work in SaaS

  • Part 1 (This Post): Idempotent Jobs & Exactly-Once Effects: Designing Safe Retries
  • Part 2: Queue Backpressure, Fairness & Tenant Isolation in Multi-Tenant SaaS
  • Part 3: Dead Letter Queues, Poison Messages & Safe Replay Playbooks
  • Part 4: Delayed Jobs, Schedulers & Clock Skew Gotchas
  • Part 5: Observability for Async Work: Correlation IDs & Job Traces
  • Part 6: Choosing Redis, SQS or Database Queues for Laravel and Node SaaS

Earlier Loop Origin series: Production MCP servers · Multi-tier caching & stampede protection · Usage-based billing metering

How do you make queue jobs safe under at-least-once delivery?

Direct answer: Assume every job can run more than once. Give each logical unit of work a stable idempotency key, record successful side effects in a dedupe store before or atomically with the effect, and make retries no-ops when that key is already completed. Exactly-once effects are designed; exactly-once delivery from the broker is not something you should bet the business on.

At-least-once is the default

Brokers and workers fail independently. A worker may finish Stripe, crash before acking the message, and another worker will process the same payload. SQS visibility timeouts, Redis requeues after SIGKILL, and database queue reserved_at reclaim all produce the same shape: duplicate execution of a job you thought was done.

That is fine for pure recomputation (rebuild a cache entry, regenerate a report file). It is not fine for:

  • Sending email or SMS
  • Charging or refunding via Stripe
  • Mutating inventory or wallet balances
  • Creating external tickets or webhooks your partners treat as unique events

Those need an exactly-once effect built on top of at-least-once delivery. The same discipline shows up in metering pipelines from the usage-based billing architecture post: count once, bill once.

Idempotency keys

An idempotency key names the business operation, not the queue attempt.

Good keys:

  • invoice:{invoice_id}:finalize
  • user:{user_id}:welcome_email:v1
  • order:{order_id}:reserve_stock
  • Stripe-style keys you already send as Idempotency-Key on the API call

Bad keys:

  • Random UUIDs generated inside handle() (every retry looks new)
  • The queue job UUID alone (re-dispatch creates a new one)
  • Timestamps

Generate the key when the command is accepted (HTTP handler, domain service), store it on the job payload, and reuse it for every attempt.

Dedupe store patterns

You need a place that remembers "this key already completed" with clear semantics.

Approach Pros Cons Best for
DB unique constraint on idempotency_key Strong, transactional with business rows Needs a table; watch long transactions Payments, inventory
Redis SET key NX EX Fast, simple TTL Must choose TTL carefully; Redis loss risk Emails, notifications
Provider idempotency (Stripe) Effect-level guarantee at the vendor Only covers that vendor call Card charges
Outbox + unique event id Ties to durable domain events More moving parts Cross-service workflows

A practical pattern for side effects:

  1. Begin transaction / acquire lock for the key.
  2. If status is completed, return success (no-op).
  3. If status is in_progress and not stale, exit and let the other worker finish (or retry later).
  4. Perform the side effect (or call Stripe with the same Idempotency-Key).
  5. Mark completed and commit.

Order matters. Marking complete before the email sends can skip a real send after a crash. Marking complete only after a non-idempotent charge can double-charge if you crash between charge and write. Prefer vendor idempotency for money; for email, accept rare duplicates or use a provider-side dedupe id.


AI-generated image.

Laravel: unique jobs and explicit keys

Laravel can prevent overlapping duplicates while a job is on the queue, which is necessary but not sufficient for exactly-once effects:

use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldBeUnique;
use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Bus\Dispatchable;
use Illuminate\Queue\InteractsWithQueue;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Mail;

class SendWelcomeEmail implements ShouldQueue, ShouldBeUnique
{
    use Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable;

    public function __construct(
        public int $userId,
        public string $idempotencyKey, // e.g. user:42:welcome_email:v1
    ) {}

    public function uniqueId(): string
    {
        return $this->idempotencyKey;
    }

    public function handle(): void
    {
        $claimed = DB::table('job_idempotency')->insertOrIgnore([
            'key' => $this->idempotencyKey,
            'status' => 'completed',
            'created_at' => now(),
            'updated_at' => now(),
        ]);

        if ($claimed === 0) {
            return; // already sent (or claimed)
        }

        $user = User::query()->findOrFail($this->userId);
        Mail::to($user)->send(new WelcomeMail($user));
    }
}

// At the HTTP edge — key is stable before dispatch
$key = "user:{$user->id}:welcome_email:v1";
SendWelcomeEmail::dispatch($user->id, $key);

ShouldBeUnique stops two welcome jobs sitting on the queue at once. The job_idempotency row stops a second send after the first succeeded and the unique lock released. For charges, call Stripe with the same key the job carries; Stripe will not create a second PaymentIntent for that Idempotency-Key.

If you are shaping Laravel services for production SaaS, the same boundaries show up in how we approach Laravel development work: commands accept idempotency keys at the edge, jobs never invent them.

Node / BullMQ equivalent 

// producer
await welcomeQueue.add(
  'welcome',
  { userId, idempotencyKey: `user:${userId}:welcome_email:v1` },
  {
    jobId: `user:${userId}:welcome_email:v1`, // BullMQ dedupe by jobId
    attempts: 5,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 },
    removeOnComplete: true,
  }
);

// worker
welcomeQueue.process(async (job) => {
  const { userId, idempotencyKey } = job.data;
  const set = await redis.set(`idem:${idempotencyKey}`, '1', 'EX', 60 * 60 * 24 * 30, 'NX');
  if (set !== 'OK') return; // already completed

  await sendWelcomeEmail(userId);
});

jobId gives you broker-level dedupe for identical enqueues. The Redis SET NX gives you effect-level dedupe across retries and re-dispatches after the original job record is gone. Mirror money moves with Stripe's Idempotency-Key header using the same string.

Cache stampede locks from the Redis/Valkey singleflight patterns are cousins of this idea: one winner does the work, everyone else observes the result.

Retry strategies compared

Strategy Behaviour Use when Risk if misused
No retry Fail once Non-critical, manually replayable Lost work
Fixed delay Retry every N seconds Simple internal APIs Thundering herd
Exponential backoff + jitter Growing delays Downstream 429/5xx Still doubles effects without keys
Unique / jobId dedupe One in-flight job per key Duplicate enqueues Does not cover post-success redelivery alone
Effect idempotency key Side effect runs once Email, payments, stock Key design bugs

Retries without idempotency keys multiply damage. Keys without retries leave users stuck on transient blips. You want both.

For broader product work that spans Laravel and Node services, the same queue contract applies across custom web application builds: define the key at command acceptance, not inside the worker.

Diagnostic checklist

  1. Can every critical job run twice without corrupting money, stock or messaging?
  2. Is the idempotency key created before dispatch and stored on the payload?
  3. Do you avoid random keys inside handle() / process callbacks?
  4. Is there a dedupe record (DB unique, Redis NX, or vendor key) for each side effect?
  5. Are Stripe (or similar) calls passing a stable Idempotency-Key?
  6. Does uniqueness middleware cover in-flight duplicates and a completed-state check?
  7. Are TTLs on Redis dedupe keys longer than any realistic late redelivery?
  8. Do poison retries go somewhere observable instead of silent infinite loops? (Part 3)
  9. Can you explain in one sentence what happens after a crash between side effect and ack?
  10. Have you load-tested duplicate delivery (replay the same payload) in staging?

FAQ

Is exactly-once delivery possible?

In general distributed systems, end-to-end exactly-once delivery is fragile. Design for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers. That combination gives you exactly-once effects where it matters.

Should every job be idempotent?

Every job with an external side effect should be. Pure recomputation can be naturally idempotent if it overwrites the same artifact. Still guard expensive LLM or vendor calls; retries without caches burn money, which is why agent and tool-cost threads keep trending.

What TTL should Redis dedupe keys use?

Longer than your maximum job retention plus any manual replay window. Thirty days is a common starting point for emails; financial keys often live in Postgres forever.

Does Laravel ShouldBeUnique replace a dedupe table?

No. It mostly prevents concurrent duplicates while a job is queued or running. After success, a re-dispatch with a new attempt still needs a completed-state check.

How do I test this?

In staging, dispatch the same job payload twice, kill a worker mid-handler, and replay DLQ messages. Assert one email, one charge, one inventory row.

What about MCP and agent tool calls?

Treat each tool invocation that mutates state like a job side effect: stable ids, dedupe, and budgets. The production MCP server patterns for approval gates pair naturally with idempotent execution.

Next in this series, Part 2 covers queue backpressure, fairness and tenant isolation so one noisy customer cannot starve everyone else's workers.

summary:
Most TLS outages I have been called into did not start with a dramatic key leak. They started with a certificate someone never really read: a missing Subject Alternative Name, an incomplete chain file, a leaf that looked fine in a browser on one machine and failed everywhere else. Browser UIs hide the details. openssl x509 -text does not. Once you can walk a certificate by hand, half of "SSL is broken" tickets become a five-minute diagnosis instead of a day of guessing.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command and example myself against current OpenSSL behaviour. I build PixelValut, a set of free browser-based developer and network tools, and this is Part 2 of the series on Web PKI and certificate forensics. Part 1 covered leaked private keys and rotation. Here we slow down and learn to read what a certificate actually asserts.

📚 Series Roadmap — Web PKI & Certificate Forensics in Practice

  • Part 2 (This Post): Reading X.509 Certificates by Hand: SANs, Key Usage, Chains & Intermediates
  • Part 3: Certificate Revocation in 2026: CRLs, the Decline of OCSP & Short-Lived Certificates
  • Part 4: Certificate Transparency Monitoring: Catching Unexpected Certificates for Your Domains
  • Part 5: ACME Automation Failures: Renewal Outages, Rate Limits & DNS-01 Pitfalls
  • Part 6: Mutual TLS for Internal APIs: Private CAs, Rotation & Pinning Trade-offs

How do you read an X.509 TLS certificate by hand?

Direct answer: Dump the leaf with openssl x509 -text, confirm Subject and Issuer, verify every hostname lives in the Subject Alternative Name extension, check Key Usage and Extended Key Usage for server auth, then walk the chain until you reach a trusted root. Most production failures are a missing intermediate or a hostname that never made it into the SAN list.

Pull the leaf and read it

Fetch what the server actually presents, not what you think is on disk:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com \
  -showcerts /dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -text

Or inspect a PEM file from your load balancer:

openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -text

You want the same fields every time. An SSL certificate checker is useful for a quick browser-side view of issuer, SANs and expiry; the OpenSSL dump is what you use when you need exact extension flags.

Subject and Issuer 

Subject: CN = example.com
Issuer: C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11

Subject is who the certificate claims to be. Issuer is who signed it. For publicly trusted TLS, the Issuer is almost always an intermediate, not the root. If Subject and Issuer are identical, you are looking at a self-signed certificate, which is fine for lab work and wrong for a public site.

SAN vs CN (the hostname trap)

Browsers and modern clients match hostnames against the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension, not against the Common Name. A certificate with CN=example.com and no SAN will fail hostname verification in current clients even when the CN "looks right."

openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -ext subjectAltName

Expect something like:

X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:example.com, DNS:www.example.com

If api.example.com is missing from that list, clients talking to api.example.com will reject the certificate regardless of how clean the chain looks. Wildcard SANs (DNS:*.example.com) cover one label only; they do not cover a.b.example.com.

Key Usage and Extended Key Usage

These extensions constrain what the key is allowed to do:

openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -ext keyUsage,extendedKeyUsage

For a public HTTPS leaf you typically want:

Extension Expected on HTTPS leaf Red flag
Key Usage Digital Signature, Key Encipherment (RSA) or Digital Signature (ECDSA) Certificate Sign / CRL Sign on a leaf
Extended Key Usage TLS Web Server Authentication Client Auth only, or empty when a client enforces EKU
basicConstraints CA:FALSE CA:TRUE on a leaf (mis-issued or wrong file)

A leaf marked CA:TRUE is either a serious CA mistake or, more often, you opened an intermediate by accident and thought it was the site certificate.

basicConstraints and path length 

openssl x509 -in intermediate.pem -noout -ext basicConstraints

Intermediates should say CA:TRUE. Leaves should say CA:FALSE or omit CA entirely depending on profile. PathLen constraints on intermediates limit how deep a chain may go; you rarely edit these by hand, but you need to recognize them when a private CA chain fails to validate.


AI-generated image.

Building and verifying the chain

TLS clients need a path from the leaf to a trust anchor they already have. Servers must send the leaf and every intermediate. They should not send the root; clients already have roots.

# Show the full chain the server sends
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com \
  -showcerts /dev/null | sed -n '/BEGIN CERTIFICATE/,/END CERTIFICATE/p'

Verify locally once you have leaf + intermediates in one PEM:

openssl verify -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt \
  -untrusted intermediates.pem leaf.pem

-untrusted is where intermediates go. If verification fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate," the usual cause is a missing intermediate in what you serve, not a broken root store.

Leaf + wrong intermediate Chain that does not link unable to get local issuer certificate

  2. Is every served hostname listed in Subject Alternative Name?
  3. Is Issuer an intermediate you recognize, not a mystery private CA on a public site?
  4. Is basicConstraints CA:FALSE (or equivalent) on the leaf?
  5. Do Key Usage / EKU allow server authentication?
  6. Does the server send intermediates (fullchain), not leaf-only?
  7. Does openssl verify succeed with your platform trust store?
  8. Are Not Before / Not After in a sensible window (clock skew included)?
  9. Does the public key type and size match your policy?
  10. Did you compare the live handshake to the files on disk after the last deploy?

Browsers sometimes cache intermediates, fetch missing ones, or use a different trust store. Command-line verify against the system store is the harsher, more portable check. Trust the stricter result for server configuration.

Profiles vary. Many CAs still set CN for compatibility, but hostname matching is SAN-based. Never rely on CN alone.

cert.pem is usually the leaf. fullchain.pem is leaf plus intermediates. Almost every reverse proxy should be pointed at the full chain file.

Not if your clients enforce it. Mutual TLS and some enterprise proxies are strict. For public HTTPS leaves, Server Auth should be present.

Often a missing intermediate: desktop browsers had it cached; mobile clients did not. Always test with a clean openssl s_client after renewal.

Prefer pinning sparingly and prefer monitoring Certificate Transparency (covered in Part 4). Intermediate replacements by public CAs are normal; hard pins without a backup plan cause outages.
