title: From One VM to a Three-Tier App, With an AI that Wouldn't Let Press Apply
summary:
Last week I built infrastructure by clicking through consoles and running commands. This week I wrote it down as code, built it again, destroyed it, and built something bigger. Five assignments, two clouds, and one rule that mattered more than any of the code: a human reviews every change before it touches the account.

Here's how the week actually went, including the apply that failed halfway.

Part 1: One file, six resources

The first assignment was the smallest: an Azure Linux VM defined entirely in Terraform. A resource group, virtual network, subnet, public IP, network interface, and the VM, all in a single main.tf.

What struck me was how little I had to describe. The NIC points at the subnet, and the VM points at the NIC. Terraform works out the build order from those references, and terraform plan showed me exactly what would be created before anything existed. That preview is the safety net the portal never gave me.

Two habits started here and stayed all week:

  • The VM password lived in a variable marked sensitive, supplied through the environment, so it never appeared in the file or in a screenshot.
  • Every build ended with terraform destroy. Create, verify, destroy.

Part 2: The same ideas on AWS

The second assignment rebuilt the pattern on AWS: a custom VPC with a public and a private subnet, an internet gateway, a public route table, a security group, and an EC2 instance that installs Nginx at boot.

It also taught me about permissions. My IAM user was read-only from an earlier audit assignment, and Terraform needs to create things. A harmless dry run caught it before I wasted any time:

aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.99.0.0/16 --dry-run

UnauthorizedOperation meant missing permission. DryRunOperation ... would have succeeded meant I was good to go. I attached the EC2 policy and moved on.

Part 3: A React app that deploys itself

The third assignment used Azure custom_data (cloud-init) to turn an empty Ubuntu VM into a running React site: install Node and Nginx, clone the repository, build it, and serve the build folder.

Two details nearly tripped me up. A script saved with Windows line endings fails silently at boot, because the first line becomes #!/bin/bash\r. And a small VM can run out of memory during npm run build, so the script creates a swap file first. Neither shows up in a tutorial, and both would have cost me an evening.

Part 4: Modules, and an apply that half-worked

The fourth assignment split an AWS build into reusable modules: network, EC2, and RDS. The root file calls each module and passes outputs between them, so the database gets its subnets and security group from the network module without anything being copied by hand.

My first apply created twelve of thirteen resources and then failed on the database. RDS rejected my master password, because it forbids characters like /, @, ", and spaces. Terraform had recorded everything it had already built, so after fixing the password, the second apply created just the one missing resource. That was my first real lesson in why state matters.

Then I connected from the EC2 instance to the private database, imported the schema, and tested a cart action in the browser to see the matching row appear in RDS.

Part 5: The capstone, with Claude Code in the loop

The capstone was a production-style three-tier deployment of a Book Review app: a VPC across two Availability Zones with six subnets, a public load balancer, a web tier running Nginx and Next.js, an internal load balancer, a private Node.js API tier, and a Multi-AZ RDS MySQL database with a read replica. Sixty-three resources in the first apply.

The assignment's real subject was the workflow. I set up Claude Code with:

  • a CLAUDE.md holding the architecture, CIDR plan, security rules, and approval rules;
  • a Terraform engineer subagent that proposes a design, reads the current provider docs through the Terraform MCP server, and then builds one phase at a time;
  • a read-only reviewer subagent that checks each phase and reports PASS, WARN, or FAIL;
  • hooks that block auto-approved changes and format code after every edit.

Claude could validate and plan. Applying and destroying were reserved for me.

The review loop earned its keep. The reviewer caught a bootstrap script that could fail before Nginx was configured, missing validation on the admin SSH range, and a subtle risk I'd have walked into: with load balancer health checks and a manual deployment, the Auto Scaling group would eventually terminate my unhealthy instances and delete my hand-deployed work. I stretched the grace period and suspended the replacement process while I deployed.

The failure no review could catch

The first capstone apply failed on the read replica:

Creating read replicas for source instance with engine mysql where ManageMasterUserPassword is enabled is not supported.

Every plan, every review, and every doc lookup had passed. Only AWS knew that rule. I gave Claude the real error and we compared options: drop the replica (the assignment required one), or generate the password in Terraform with a write-only argument and store it in Secrets Manager, so it never lands in state or outputs. The plan showed the primary updating in place, and the second apply finished the replica.

It's a clean illustration of what the Terraform MCP server is and isn't. It serves documentation. It can't query my account, so it couldn't predict this.

I also said no to a recommendation. Claude suggested an instance refresh for the change, but nothing was deployed yet, so the refresh would have waited on replacements that couldn't become healthy. I replaced the two App instances myself with one command instead.

Deploying by hand, then proving it

User data only installed software, so I deployed the apps myself: the backend through a systemd service that fetches its database password from Secrets Manager at start, and the frontend built on each web instance. Both target groups went healthy, I registered a user, wrote a review, and then read both rows back from the private database. The credentials came from the instance's IAM role, so no password ever appeared in a terminal.

Then terraform destroy. A NAT gateway, two load balancers, and three database instances bill by the hour, and the most important command of the week was the last one.

What I'm taking away

  • State is the memory. A failed apply isn't a disaster, because Terraform resumes from what it recorded. Guard the state file, and never delete the project folder before you destroy.
  • AI is a fast engineer and a careful reviewer, but it can't see your live account. The best results came from a loop: plan, research, build, validate, review, then a human decides.
  • Keep secrets out of everything. Sensitive variables, write-only arguments, Secrets Manager, and a rule that nothing credential-shaped goes into user data or outputs.
  • Test each layer in order. Every deployment problem this week was solved by checking one hop at a time, not guessing.
  • Treat cost as part of the design. A single NAT gateway and a short-lived environment were deliberate tradeoffs, and I could explain every one of them.

title: Invalid Host header after deploying? Why it happens and the fix
summary:
By Octave · drafted with AI, tested on Hubfly space. Originally published on the Hubfly space blog.

TL;DR

  • What you get: the exact error each framework prints when it rejects your public address, the one-line fix for each, and a 10-second curl check to catch it before you deploy.
  • Who it's for: anyone who just put a Vite, React, Vue, Django or MCP server app online and got a blank 403, 400 or 421 instead of their page.
  • Time needed: 10–15 minutes.

Checked in October 2026 with Vite 8, webpack-dev-server 6, Django 6.1 and the Python MCP SDK 2.x.

Your app worked on localhost. You deployed it, opened the public URL, and got a one-line page: Invalid Host header. Or Blocked request. This host is not allowed. Or a bare Bad Request (400) with nothing in the logs.

Nothing is broken on the server. Your app is refusing visitors on purpose, because it doesn't recognise the address they typed. In this guide you'll make your app accept its real address, and only that address, so your site loads and stays protected. It takes one setting per framework.

Try it on Hubfly space: you get a free HTTPS address for your app on the free tier (360 hours a month, no card).

Why your app rejects its own address

Every browser request carries a Host header: the name the visitor typed, like shop-web.eu1.hubfly.app. On your laptop that name is always localhost or 127.0.0.1. Once you're online, the platform's edge proxy handles HTTPS and passes the public name through to your container unchanged.

Browser ──Host: shop-web.eu1.hubfly.app──▶ HTTPS proxy ──same Host──▶ your container
                                                                  │
                                         "Is this name on my list?" ┘
                                          no → 403 / 400 / 421

Many dev servers and frameworks keep a list of names they'll answer to. By default that list is only localhost. This protects you from DNS rebinding, an attack where a malicious website tricks a browser into talking to a server it shouldn't reach. So the check is good. It just doesn't know your new name yet.

Each tool fails differently, which is why the error is so confusing:

What you run What visitors see Status Where it's logged
Vite dev server (vite) Blocked request. This host ("…") is not allowed. 403 Not in server output
vite preview Same message, pointing at preview.allowedHosts 403 Not in server output
webpack-dev-server (Vue CLI, older React and Angular setups) Invalid Host header 403 Not in server output
Django with DEBUG = False Bad Request (400) 400 Nowhere by default
Python MCP SDK (streamable_http_app()) Invalid Host header 421 WARNING Invalid Host header: …

The same request, four tools, four different answers.

Step 1: Reproduce it on your laptop in 10 seconds

You don't need to deploy to see the error. Start your app locally, then send it the public name with curl:

# Replace the port and the name with yours
curl -i -H "Host: your-app.eu1.hubfly.app" http://127.0.0.1:5173/

If you get a 403, 400 or 421, you've found the problem without waiting for a deploy. Keep this command handy: you'll run it again after each fix.

Why this works: the check only looks at the Host header, not at how the request reached your app. Faking the header locally triggers exactly what your visitors see.

Step 2: Stop running a dev server in production (frontends)

If the error comes from Vite or webpack-dev-server, the real fix is usually not a setting. It's that you deployed the development server. Dev servers rebuild on every change, use more memory, and carry these local-only safety checks.

Build your site once and serve the static files instead. For a Vite app (React, Vue, Svelte, Solid), add a static file server:

npm install sirv-cli

Then set your scripts in package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "start": "sirv dist --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT:-8080} --single"
  }
}

Your platform runs npm run build once, then npm start. A static file server has no host check, so the error disappears. --single sends unknown paths like /orders/42 to index.html, which single-page apps need for client-side routing. --host 0.0.0.0 makes the server reachable from outside the container. (Binding to 127.0.0.1 instead gives you a 502; see our guide to the 502 Bad Gateway fix.)

On Hubfly space, set the container port to the one in your start script (8080 here).

Step 3: When you do need the check, allow your real name

Sometimes you really do want the server running online: a shared preview, a Django app, an MCP server. Then add your public name to the allowlist. List the exact names. Never switch the check off.

Vite (dev and preview) 

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'

const hosts = (process.env.ALLOWED_HOSTS || '').split(',').filter(Boolean)

export default defineConfig({
  server: { host: '0.0.0.0', allowedHosts: hosts },
})

Set ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-app.eu1.hubfly.app in the environment. A leading dot allows a domain and all its subdomains: .your-domain.com covers staging.your-domain.com too. vite preview uses server.allowedHosts unless you set preview.allowedHosts separately, so one list covers both.

Don't use allowedHosts: true. It accepts any name, which turns the protection off.

webpack-dev-server (Vue CLI and custom webpack setups) 

// webpack.config.js
module.exports = {
  // ...
  devServer: {
    host: '0.0.0.0',
    allowedHosts: ['your-app.eu1.hubfly.app', '.your-domain.com'],
  },
};

The same leading-dot rule applies. Old answers suggest disableHostCheck: true or allowedHosts: 'all'. The first was removed in webpack-dev-server 4 (current versions refuse to start with it), and the second turns the check off.

Django: two settings, not one

Django has two checks, and the second only shows up after you fix the first.

1. ALLOWED_HOSTS blocks unknown names with Bad Request (400). With DEBUG = False, Django logs this through its mail_admins handler only. Gunicorn's output stays empty, which is why this one feels like a ghost. Read the list from the environment:

# settings.py
import os

ALLOWED_HOSTS = [h for h in os.environ.get("ALLOWED_HOSTS", "").split(",") if h]
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = [o for o in os.environ.get("CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS", "").split(",") if o]

2. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS matters as soon as someone submits a form, including the admin login. The platform's proxy handles HTTPS and talks to your app over plain HTTP inside the network. So the browser says the request came from https://your-app…, Django thinks it's serving http://your-app…, and every POST fails with 403 CSRF verification failed. With DEBUG = True the page shows the real reason: Origin checking failed - https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app does not match any trusted origins.

Set both values in your container's environment:

ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-app.eu1.hubfly.app
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app

Note the difference: ALLOWED_HOSTS takes bare names, while CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS needs the scheme (https://).

To make the next host error visible in your logs, send Django's host warnings to the console:

LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "handlers": {"console": {"class": "logging.StreamHandler"}},
    "loggers": {
        "django.security.DisallowedHost": {"handlers": ["console"], "level": "ERROR"},
    },
}

Now an unknown name prints Invalid HTTP_HOST header: 'your-app.eu1.hubfly.app'. You may need to add 'your-app.eu1.hubfly.app' to ALLOWED_HOSTS. in your container logs.

Python MCP server: the 421 error

The official Python MCP SDK switches on host checking when the app is built for 127.0.0.1, which is the default for streamable_http_app(). Running it with uvicorn ... host="0.0.0.0" doesn't change that, so your public URL gets 421 Invalid Host header while curl localhost works fine.

Pass your public name explicitly:

import os
import uvicorn
from mcp.server import MCPServer
from mcp.server.transport_security import TransportSecuritySettings

mcp = MCPServer("orders")

@mcp.tool()
def ping() -> str:
    return "pong"

public_host = os.environ["PUBLIC_HOST"]  # e.g. your-mcp.eu1.hubfly.app

app = mcp.streamable_http_app(
    transport_security=TransportSecuritySettings(
        allowed_hosts=[public_host],
        allowed_origins=[f"https://{public_host}"],
    )
)

uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

Your public name now gets a normal response, and any other name still gets 421. That includes 127.0.0.1: if a local health check calls the server, add 127.0.0.1:8000 to allowed_hosts too. The SDK's own mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="0.0.0.0") skips the host check entirely; only use it if the server sits behind an access key. For the full MCP setup with HTTPS and an access key, see Deploy your own MCP server.

Step 4: Put the name in your environment on Hubfly space

Keep the hostname out of your code so the same build works for staging, production and your own domain.

  1. Open your project in the Hubfly space dashboard and create or open your container.
  2. Go to Network → Add Domain → Auto Endpoint. You get an HTTPS address like your-app.eu1.hubfly.app, with TLS and force-HTTPS switched on.
  3. Copy that address. Under Configuration → Environment Variables, add ALLOWED_HOSTS (and for Django, CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS with https:// in front).
  4. Redeploy or restart the container so the app reads the new values.

The Environment Variables tab with both values set.

Adding your own domain later? Add it to the same variables, separated by a comma: ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-app.eu1.hubfly.app,www.your-domain.com. For a custom domain, add the DNS record the dashboard shows; Hubfly space issues the certificate and renews it 30 days before it expires.

Step 5: Check it

Open your public URL in the browser, or run:

curl -i https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app/

Once your name is on the list, you get your page instead of a 403, 400 or 421. Then try a name you didn't allow, against your local copy:

curl -i -H "Host: not-mine.example.com" http://127.0.0.1:8000/

That one should still be refused. If both behave, the fix is done and the protection is still on.

What can go wrong

1. "I fixed ALLOWED_HOSTS, now the admin login says CSRF verification failed."

That's the second Django check. Add CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app, with the scheme. If your proxy sets X-Forwarded-Proto, SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER is the other route, but only use it when the proxy always overwrites that header. Otherwise a client could fake it.

2. "I added the name, but it's still blocked."

Check what you typed against the error text: www.your-domain.com and your-domain.com are different names. In Vite and webpack a leading dot covers subdomains; without the dot it matches one exact name. Also check the app actually restarted: dev servers and Django read these settings at startup.

3. "It works on the platform URL but not my custom domain."

Each name your visitors use must be on the list. Add the custom domain (and www, if you use it) to ALLOWED_HOSTS, and to CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS with https:// for Django.

4. "It works, but my bundle is huge and the page is slow."

You're probably still running the dev server. Go back to Step 2 and serve the built files.

Takeaway

"Invalid Host header" means your app's safety check doesn't know its new name. For frontends, the best fix is to stop shipping the dev server and serve your build. For everything else, put your exact public name in an environment variable and feed it to the framework's allowlist. Never turn the check off. And before your next deploy, run one curl -H "Host: …" locally: it catches the problem in 10 seconds.
